cost.typical: Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $9,000–$24,000 on a full asphalt-shingle roof replacement. Where you land depends on the roof’s size and pitch, how many old layers come off, and the shingle line you choose.

rows.note: The most common job — tear-off and replace on a typical 1,800–2,400 sq ft roof in mid-range architectural (dimensional) shingles.

rows.job: Roof repair (leak, flashing, a few shingles)
rows.note: Localized fixes — chimney flashing, a slipped course, or a small active leak.
How roofers actually quote a job. Multiply by your roof’s squares for a rough total.
A 40–50 year roof in premium material and labor — common on modern and barn-style homes.
Specialty craftsmanship for period-correct restorations on older Fairfield County homes.

cost.factors: roof pitch and height (steeper and taller cost more), how many old layers are torn off, skylights and chimneys to flash around, and any gutter, fascia, or decking repair found once the old roof is off
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Any roofer working on a Connecticut home needs an active Home Improvement Contractor registration plus their own liability and workers'-comp coverage. Ask to see both before work starts.

guide.t: Get the full scope in writing
guide.d: Tear-off vs. going over the old layer, underlayment, flashing, ice-and-water shield, ventilation, and cleanup each change the price and the result. A one-line quote hides the parts that matter.

guide.t: Ask about the manufacturer warranty
guide.d: A factory warranty (GAF, CertainTeed, Owens Corning) only holds if the installer is certified and follows spec. Certified shops can often register a longer warranty in your name.

guide.t: Be wary of pressure and 'today-only' pricing
guide.d: Storm-chasers and rush discounts are red flags. A reputable roofer gives you a written estimate and the time to decide.

cost.typical: Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $6,000–$14,000 to replace a central heating or cooling system. Where you land depends on the size your home needs, the efficiency rating you choose, and whether your existing ductwork can be reused.

rows.note: The most common cooling job — replacing an aging system on existing ductwork. Tonnage and SEER2 efficiency drive the spread.
Swapping a worn furnace. High-efficiency (96%+ AFUE) and variable-speed units sit at the top of the range.
Increasingly common for electrification. Cold-climate models and multi-zone setups cost more.
Priced per indoor head — ideal for additions, sunrooms, and homes without ductwork.

rows.job: Service call, tune-up, or minor repair
rows.note: A tech visit, refrigerant top-off, capacitor, or thermostat — not a full replacement.

cost.factors: the size (tonnage / BTU) your home actually needs, the efficiency rating you choose (SEER2 / AFUE), whether existing ductwork can be reused, electrical upgrades for heat pumps, and how easy the equipment is to reach
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Ask for a load calculation, not a guess
guide.d: The right-sized system comes from a Manual-J load calc on your actual home — not 'same as the old one.' Oversized units short-cycle, run loud, and cost more to own.

guide.t: Confirm the CT license
guide.d: Heating and cooling work is done under a Connecticut HVAC license. The licensed technician — not just the company name — is who is accountable for the install.

guide.t: Get equipment, permit, and warranty in writing
guide.d: Model and efficiency (SEER2 / AFUE), the permit, and warranty registration should all be itemized. A permit and post-install inspection protect you.

guide.t: Check real emergency response
guide.d: When heat or AC fails, a callback in hours beats a cheaper shop that goes quiet in a cold snap. Ask their honest after-hours window before you need it.

cost.typical: Plumbing spans tiny fixes to full repipes, so the range is wide. Most service jobs land between $200 and $1,200, while big-ticket replacements — water heater, repipe, or sewer line — run into the thousands.

rows.job: Service call / common repair (leak, faucet, running toilet)
rows.note: The most common job — a visit plus a straightforward fix.
A standard gas or electric tank, installed and hauled away. Tankless costs more.
A gas tankless unit including venting and any gas-line work.
Highly excavation-dependent. Trenchless lining sits at the top of the range.
Replacing aging galvanized or polybutylene supply lines with PEX or copper.

cost.factors: whether the work is accessible or buried behind walls and underground, fixture and material grade (PEX vs copper), permit and inspection requirements, and whether it is an emergency or a scheduled job
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Verify the CT plumbing license
guide.d: Plumbing is performed under a Connecticut P-class license held by the individual tradesperson. Confirm it is active before anyone touches a pipe.

guide.t: Insist on an itemized estimate
guide.d: Parts, labor, and any wall or finish repair should be listed separately. Open-ended 'time and materials' can balloon on larger jobs.

guide.t: Know the emergency rate up front
guide.d: Burst pipes and failed water heaters never wait for business hours. Ask the after-hours rate and callback window in advance.

guide.t: Get the warranty terms
guide.d: On a water heater, repipe, or fixture, ask how long parts and labor are covered — and whether the manufacturer warranty needs registering in your name.

cost.typical: Most electrical work is smaller service jobs in the $200–$1,500 range, while panel upgrades, rewires, and generators are the big-ticket items that climb into the thousands.

rows.job: Service call / common repair (outlet, switch, fixture)
rows.note: The most common job — a visit plus a defined fix or install.
Upgrading an older or overloaded panel, including the meter swap and permit.
A 240V circuit for home charging. Distance from the panel — and any panel upgrade — moves the number.
Replacing knob-and-tube or aluminum wiring in an older Fairfield County home.
A permanently wired backup generator with transfer switch and gas hookup.

cost.factors: the age and condition of existing wiring, panel capacity and whether it needs upgrading, permit and inspection requirements, and how far new circuits have to run from the panel
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Confirm the CT license and the permit
guide.d: Electrical work runs under a Connecticut E-class license, and most jobs need a permit and inspection. Both protect your home and your insurance.

guide.t: Don't shop on price alone
guide.d: The cheapest panel swap or rewire can skip grounding, AFCI/GFCI protection, or proper load math. Ask exactly what is included to code.

guide.t: Name the scope
guide.d: Panel size in amps, circuits added, fixture vs. rough-in work, and who patches the walls should all be written down before work begins.

guide.t: Match the pro to specialty work
guide.d: EV chargers, generators, and solar tie-ins each have their own requirements. Confirm hands-on experience with your specific job.

cost.typical: Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $4,000–$12,000 on a new asphalt driveway. The spread comes from size, how much old surface comes off, and whether you choose asphalt or pavers.

rows.note: The most common job — a typical residential driveway, torn out and repaved.
A fresh top layer over a sound base, or patching problem areas.
A protective coat that extends a driveway’s life — recommended every few years.
Interlocking concrete or brick pavers — premium curb appeal and longevity.
Solving water and slope problems before or during the paving job.

cost.factors: square footage, removal of the old surface, base preparation and drainage, material choice (asphalt vs pavers), and how easily equipment can reach the site
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Confirm registration and insurance
guide.d: A driveway or walkway is home-improvement work — the contractor should hold an active CT registration and carry liability coverage.

guide.t: Ask about the base, not just the surface
guide.d: Most paving failures start underneath. Ask about excavation depth, gravel base, and compaction — the part you can't inspect once it's done.

guide.t: Specify materials and thickness
guide.d: Asphalt thickness, paver brand and type, edge restraint, and drainage slope decide whether it lasts five years or twenty-five. Get them in writing.

guide.t: Mind the weather and the warranty
guide.d: Temperature affects how asphalt and joints set, so avoid marginal-weather pours. Ask what is guaranteed and for how long.

cost.typical: Lawn care is usually billed per visit or per season. Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $150–$400 a month in season, while one-time projects like a new lawn run higher.

rows.note: The most common service — a typical residential lot, mowed and trimmed.
A season of scheduled treatments, billed as a package.
Leaf removal, bed cleanup, and seasonal cutbacks.
Grading and establishing a new lawn. Sod costs more than seed.
Beds, plantings, and hardscape edging — varies widely with scope.

cost.factors: lot size, how often you want service, the condition of the existing lawn, and add-ons like irrigation, planting beds, or tree work
cost.basis: prevailing Fairfield County service rates for residential lawn care

guide.t: Match the service to your yard
guide.d: Mowing, fertilization, design and installs, and tree work are different skills. Confirm the crew actually does the work you need — not just the easy parts.

guide.t: Ask about pesticide credentials
guide.d: In Connecticut, anyone applying pesticides commercially must be registered with DEEP. If chemical treatment is part of the plan, ask who is certified.

guide.t: Put the schedule and scope in writing
guide.d: Visit frequency, what each visit covers, and seasonal cleanups should be spelled out so 'lawn care' isn't left open-ended.

guide.t: Confirm insurance for the heavy work
guide.d: Tree removal, grading, and hardscape carry real risk. Liability coverage protects you if something goes wrong on your property.

cost.typical: Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $3,000–$8,000 to repaint an interior, while a full exterior repaint runs higher. Square footage, prep, and paint grade drive where you land.

rows.note: The most common job — walls, ceilings, and trim throughout, with prep and two coats.
A bedroom or living room, including prep and two coats.
Prep, priming, and two coats. Siding type and house height drive the spread.
Sanding, priming, and spraying kitchen cabinets — a popular alternative to replacement.
Smaller defined scopes priced on their own.

cost.factors: square footage and ceiling height, how much prep and surface repair is needed, paint grade, the number of colors, and exterior access (ladders vs lifts)
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Interior and exterior painting is home-improvement work — the painter should hold an active Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor registration and carry liability coverage. Ask to see both before work starts.

guide.t: Get the prep and number of coats in writing
guide.d: Most of a paint job's lifespan is decided before the color goes on — washing, scraping, sanding, patching, priming, and how many finish coats. A one-line quote hides the part that makes it last.

guide.t: Ask about surface repair and lead-safe work
guide.d: Wood rot, failed caulk, and drywall cracks should be fixed first, not painted over. On homes built before 1978, ask whether the crew follows EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices when sanding or scraping.

guide.t: Pin down products, color, and warranty
guide.d: Paint line and finish, who supplies it, color approval, and daily cleanup should all be spelled out — along with how long the work is guaranteed and any touch-up window.

cost.typical: Masonry is priced by the project and varies widely. Most Fairfield County homeowners spend roughly $2,000–$15,000 depending on whether it’s a repair or new stonework, and on the material.

rows.note: The most common job — tuckpointing mortar joints or replacing damaged brick.
From crown and flashing repair to a full above-the-roof rebuild.
A new patio in concrete pavers or natural stone, including base prep.
Engineered block or natural stone. Height and drainage drive the cost.
Facing a foundation or wall, rebuilding front steps, or laying a stone walkway.

cost.factors: the material (brick, block, concrete paver, or natural stone), how much demolition and base prep is needed, wall height or structural requirements, and how easily the site can be reached
cost.basis: industry installed-cost ranges adjusted for Fairfield County labor rates

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Masonry, hardscape, and chimney work is home-improvement work — the mason should hold an active Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor registration and carry liability coverage. Ask to see both before any demolition starts.

guide.t: Get base prep and drainage in writing
guide.d: Patios, walkways, and walls last or fail on what is underneath — excavation depth, a compacted gravel base, and how water is directed away. A quote that only describes the visible stone hides the part that decides longevity.

guide.t: Match the material and the repair to the house
guide.d: Ask which stone, brick, or paver and what pattern, and on older or historic homes, how new work and mortar will match the existing. For chimneys and foundations, confirm whether they are rebuilding or repairing — and why.

guide.t: Pin down permits, timeline, and cleanup
guide.d: Belgian-block aprons and structural walls can require local permits — confirm who pulls them. Spell out the schedule, site protection, daily cleanup, and how long the work is guaranteed.

guide.t: Insurance first — this is the one trade where it decides everything
guide.d: Tree work is the riskiest job that happens on a home lot. Ask for current liability AND workers'-comp certificates from the insurer, not a photocopy — if an uninsured climber is hurt on your property, the claim can land on you.

guide.t: Ask about the CT arborist license for tree care
guide.d: Connecticut licenses arborists through DEEP — pruning, cabling, and treating trees for hire is licensed work. Straight removals sit outside the license, but for anything meant to keep a tree healthy, ask whether a licensed arborist is on the job.

guide.t: Get the full scope in writing
guide.d: Removal vs. pruning, whether the stump is ground out, what happens to the wood and brush, lawn and driveway protection, and whether a crane is needed — each changes the price. A one-line "take the tree down" quote hides all of it.

guide.t: Be wary of storm-chasers
guide.d: Crews that knock on the door after a storm, quote cash-only, or push same-day decisions are the classic red flag in this trade. A reputable crew gives a written estimate — even in an emergency.

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Flooring installation and refinishing is home-improvement work — the installer should hold an active Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor registration and carry liability coverage. Ask to see both before work starts.

guide.t: Get the prep underfoot in writing
guide.d: A floor lasts or fails on what is beneath it — moisture testing, subfloor repair and leveling, acclimating the wood before install. A quote that only prices the visible boards hides the part that decides whether they cup, gap, or squeak later.

guide.t: Refinish vs. replace is the real first question
guide.d: Solid hardwood can usually be sanded and refinished for a fraction of replacement — but not always, and engineered floors only take so many sandings. Ask the installer to make the case for the path they quote, not just price one.

guide.t: Pin down dust, finish, and the timeline
guide.d: Sanding is disruptive — ask about dust containment, which finish (oil vs. water-based changes cure time and smell), how long before furniture goes back, and who moves it. Spell out cleanup and the warranty on both material and labor.

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Window and door replacement is home-improvement work — the installer should hold an active Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor registration and carry liability coverage. Ask to see both before work starts.

guide.t: Ask who actually installs it
guide.d: Some window sellers subcontract installation to whoever is available that week. Ask whether the crew is in-house, and who is named to lead your specific job.

guide.t: Pin down the product line and glass spec
guide.d: Brand, series, glazing (double vs. triple pane), and low-E or gas-fill options change both price and performance. Get the exact spec in writing, not just "energy-efficient windows."

guide.t: Nail down measurements before ordering
guide.d: Custom windows and doors are made to the measurement taken — a mistake here means weeks of delay waiting on a remake. Ask who re-verifies measurements before the order is placed.

guide.t: Confirm CT registration & insurance
guide.d: Pool construction and major renovation is home-improvement work — the firm should hold an active Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor registration and carry liability coverage. Ask to see both before signing.

guide.t: Get permits and the C-of-O in writing
guide.d: Unpermitted or incomplete-permit pool builds surface at home sale, sometimes years later, and can block a closing. Ask who files the permit, get the certificate of occupancy in the contract, and confirm it before final payment.

guide.t: Pin down the build type and scope
guide.d: Gunite, fiberglass, and vinyl liner pools differ sharply in cost, timeline, and what a renovation later requires. Get the exact spec, decking and coping scope, and equipment brand in writing — not just "a new pool."

guide.t: Ask what a season of service actually costs
guide.d: A weekly-maintenance quote often excludes chemicals, opening, and closing. Ask what is included in the base price versus billed separately before the season starts.
